prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that enabled incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B021 is the one candidate on which all six of us placed first, but I do not rest the case on that agreement. On the merits it is a rare complete arc from hormone physiology (the incretin effect, proglucagon processing, GLP-1(7-36) as the active insulinotropic peptide) to drugs that now treat type 2 diabetes and obesity, with large outcome trials showing cardiovascular and renal benefit. The mechanism has been confirmed independently for three decades, so maturity is not in question, and the patient impact is among the largest of any recent advance. A three-person prize of Holst (human incretin physiology), Drucker (GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and receptor pharmacology) and Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active peptide) rewards the discoveries and not the drug engineering.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Three seats cannot cover Holst, Drucker, Mojsov, Knudsen and the Habener group, which is not on our credit list, and Mojsov's share is the most contested name in the configuration. Leaving out Knudsen, whose acylated analogues made once-weekly dosing possible, is defensible on a discovery-versus-development basis but is not obviously fair given where the clinical benefit actually comes from. If the committee decides the priority record for the active peptide cannot be settled, the prize could be narrowed or delayed, and I would then turn to B022 or B001, which have cleaner attribution but less clinical reach.

responses.point: Drucker, Holst and Mojsov are a plausible three-person set, Knudsen is a fourth-seat issue, and the Habener credit dispute cannot be resolved from the supplied text.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and on treating Knudsen as a development contribution outside the three seats. I would go further on Habener. Leaving him off means we are choosing a side in the peptide-identification dispute, not simply trimming a list. That is a reason to word the citation around GLP-1 physiology and its active form and to avoid a claim about who first found the peptide. I also differ with you on B012. You rank TNF blockade third and call it overdue. I rank it third as well, but I would not let its maturity push it ahead of the cleaner mechanistic cases while Cerami, Vilcek and Kollias remain uncredited.

responses.point: The GLP-1 trio is timely, but Mojsov's share is the part most contested in his recollection; he also ranks cGAS-STING sixth and limits it to Chen and Barber.
responses.response: I take the Mojsov concern seriously, and it is the main reason I keep an alternative in reserve. But the contest is about priority, not about whether her identification and synthesis of the active peptide was essential, and a committee can describe that contribution without adjudicating who was first. On cGAS-STING, I rank it second, while you place it sixth because translation is not yet established. I accept that point and treat it as the real weakness of B001. Still, interferon-driven disease and STING-associated vasculopathy give it more human-disease grounding than a purely mechanistic pathway, and I would not put it below optogenetics on medical relevance.

responses.point: He ranks SMN2 antisense correction (B007) second, as a coherent Krainer and Bennett pair that is mechanistically clear, clinically robust and timely.
responses.response: I rank B007 fourth and share your view that it is a landmark for RNA-targeted medicine. I disagree that it should outrank B022 or B001 as the lead alternative. The Krainer and Bennett pairing is clean, but the SMN gene discovery (Lefebvre, Melki) and the work defining the ISS-N1 target are outside the credit, so the chain from mechanism to drug is told from only part of its start. I also see a risk that B007 is read as an award for a modality, antisense chemistry, in which Bennett's role is carried by the drug program. That makes it a stronger candidate for a later year than for a second part now.

responses.point: He puts imatinib and BCR-ABL inhibition (B045) second and calls its importance, clarity and lasting impact exceptional.
responses.response: B045 is fully mature and the clinical impact is not in doubt, but I did not rank it, and I do not think the committee should reach it by default. Its weakness is the line between foundational discovery and drug development. Rowley, Nowell and Hungerford, and the Witte and Baltimore ABL work, are not credited, and the three names on the ballot are all drug-development and clinical translation. For a physiology or medicine prize that is the same difficulty we face with Knudsen in B021. If we apply that framing consistently I would not move B045 ahead of the basic-mechanism cases.

responses.point: He ranks CAR-T cells (B052) second, with June and Sadelain central and Rosenberg for adoptive cell therapy, noting uncredited contributors such as Eshhar.
responses.response: I agree that CAR-T is a new therapeutic modality with durable responses in refractory B-cell malignancies. But your own attribution note undercuts the case for now. The chimeric receptor concept came from Eshhar, who is not credited, and the field is moving into autoimmunity, where long-term safety and durability are unsettled. I would be reluctant to set a prize on a story whose third chapter is still being written. I can see it ranked higher in a later year, but I do not see it displacing B021 now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can settle the priority record for the active GLP-1 peptide (Mojsov versus Habener) well enough to credit Mojsov without distortion.
Whether Knudsen should be preferred to Mojsov or Drucker if development contributions are weighted more heavily.
Whether the lead alternative should be cGAS-STING (more disease relevance, translation still early) or UPR (cleaner attribution, less direct clinical impact).
I am working from recollection of the historical literature and not from verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B021, B022 or B001. My research field (autoimmunity, rheumatology, type I interferon) is close to B012 and B001, but that is topical overlap and not a personal tie. For B012 I would still flag the subject-area closeness to the committee. The recorded co-authors (Kuchroo, Sonesson) and my Bergen affiliation are not linked to any shortlisted candidate.
